newsitem.title: USA: U.S. tax bill to face line-item veto review.
newsitem.headline: U.S. tax bill to face line-item veto review.

text.p: The $95 billion tax-cut bill passed by Congress will undergo a White House review for possible use of President Bill Clinton's line-item veto authority, White House spokesman Mike McCurry said on Friday.
McCurry did not rule out the possibility that Clinton would use the line-item veto, authorised by a law which took effect in January.
But any exercise of the line-item veto would not violate the fundamental bipartisan agreements made in reaching the balanced budget deal this week, McCurry said.

"I'm not ruling anything in or out," McCurry said, referring to use of the veto. "I'm not suggesting at all that the president intends to exercise line-item veto in any of those provisions. That analysis will begin once the bill is received by the White House," he told reporters.
"The president will remain faithful to the (budget) agreement," he said later.
McCurry said he could not speculate on the fate of specific provisions in the tax bill, passed as part of a budget-balancing agreement reached earlier in the week.

Asked if the Clinton would veto special interest provisions he found objectionable, McCurry said, "If the president finds something that's veto-able under these provisions, I don't think he would hesitate to use his authority."
McCurry said the White House review would be run by the National Economic Council, including the Office of Management and Budget and the Treasury.

The tax legislation passed by both houses of Congress on Thursday is the first tax bill to face the possibility of such a veto. The line-item authority allows the president to strip items from spending and tax measures without vetoing an entire bill.
The Supreme Court dismissed a legal challenge to the law in June.
Under the line-item veto law, Congress must identify for review tax breaks that apply only to a limited number of taxpayers.
There are roughly 80 such provisions in the pending tax bill, McCurry said.
The president, after signing the overall legislation, has five days in which to strike objectionable provisions that are subject to the law.
Congress can override any line-item veto by a two-thirds majority in each house.
Clinton is to sign the balanced budget legislation at a White House ceremony on Tuesday, McCurry said.
